Three goods, three people, each owning one good. The triangle holds every set of relative prices; its center is the only equilibrium. The arrows show how the classical adjustment moves the prices: up where a good is in excess demand.
Let time rise off the page. With one representative consumer the prices go to the center and then climb straight up it: equilibrium, reached.
In Scarf’s economy each person wants a different pair of goods. The same adjustment carries the prices round the center, climbing, and never closer to it.

The equilibrium exists in both: a fixed-point theorem from topology guarantees it. Whether it is reached depends on how unlike the people are, and Sonnenschein, Mantel and Debreu showed that adding up unlike people puts almost no shape on total demand.

Does a minimum wage cost jobs? In a competitive market, a floor above the competitive wage of {0} cuts employment. Where the employer sets the wage, a floor between what it would pay and {1} raises employment. Two answers, one for each hand.
What decides between them is held still in each drawing: the employer’s power to set the wage, μ. Fold it up as an axis.
Between the two lines a surface fills in: employment for every floor and every degree of power.

On it, the sign of the effect changes along two lines. Above what the employer would pay and below the competitive wage, a higher floor adds jobs. Past the competitive wage it costs jobs, whatever μ is.

The economist’s answer is therefore a condition, not a sign: which side of the line the actual market is on. That is measurable. Card and Krueger ({0}) compared fast-food employment in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage, with neighboring Pennsylvania, which did not, and found no fall.
On the wheel the minimum wage is a held value of regulation, and the labor market moves. The two hands are two regions of one surface, and a design tells which one we are in.

That number is the core’s answer, drawn as a line across every degree of capital mobility, as if mobility did not matter.

The plan of the archive: four layers of what economics studies, six cells each, and every name a door to the course that teaches it.
Roll the plan up and each layer is a ring of one wheel, Frank Knight’s wheel of wealth ({0}). Build it from the rim in. First the agents, where everything that circulates starts and ends.

Then the markets, where agents meet: goods, labor, money, capital, foreign exchange, and the land and air that have no market until one is made. What the agents send one another starts to circulate through them; each route first carries one parcel alone.
Then the institutions, the rules the agents meet under. Taxes start to flow through theirs.
At the hub, the methods. They are not in the economy: they are the tools every other ring is read with, and Part {0} added one at five of its stages.

Six of them Part {0} relaxes itself: price-taking at strategy, full information at contracts, complete markets in the land and air, equilibrium at once in the labor market, consistent choice among households, and data that speak for themselves at measurement.
Two it never relaxes head-on. The first is the representative agent: one firm stands for all firms, one household for all households. Drawn that way, every firm on the wheel is the same size.
Relaxed, the firms are as unequal as Zipf’s law says, a few giants and a long tail, and households differ in income too.
The second is no connections: any household buys from any firm, through the market.
Relaxed, each household is tied to a few firms, firms to their suppliers, banks to one another, and what moves travels along the ties.
